'''Tamayori-bime''' ({{lang|ja|玉依毘売}}) or '''Tamayori-hime''' ({{lang|ja|玉依姫}}) is in origin a common noun, a general title meaning "a woman possessed by a divine spirit", a shamaness who is possessed by and married to a god. In ancient myths and traditions many women who bore children to gods are called by it.<ref name="kotobank">{{cite web |title=玉依姫 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/玉依姫 |website=Kotobank |language=ja}}</ref><ref name="kokugakuin">{{cite web |title=Tamayoribime |url=https://kojiki.kokugakuin.ac.jp/shinmei/tamayoribime/ |website=Kojiki Database of Divine Names |publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref> This article is about the Tamayori-hime of [[Japanese mythology]] known as the mother of [[Emperor Jimmu]]: Tamayori-bime in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and Tamayori-hime in the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]''.

She is the daughter of the sea god [[Watatsumi]] and the younger sister of [[Toyotama-hime]]. When Toyotama-hime left her husband [[Hoori]], Tamayori-hime raised their son [[Ugayafukiaezu]]; when he grew up he married her, his aunt, and she bore him four sons, the youngest of whom became Emperor Jimmu, the first emperor of Japan.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Allan |first1=Tony |last2=Phillips |first2=Charles |last3=Kerrigan |first3=Michael |title=Realm of the Rising Sun: Japanese Myth |date=2000 |publisher=[[Time-Life Books]] |isbn=9780705436632 |pages=68–69}}</ref>

== Overview ==
The name Tamayori-hime is found for other, separate figures in the ''Kiki'' myths and the ''[[Fudoki]]'' as well as for this one.<ref name="kotobank"/> According to Kuratsuka Akiko, Tamayori-hime means "a woman to whom a divine spirit attaches", and is "the shamaness who attends the secret rite of the god's descent at a festival, given mythical form as the mother who conceives by the god and bears his child". In the stories it is treated as a proper name, the name of a particular goddess or woman, but it is more correctly understood as a common noun, a general title.<ref name="kotobank"/><ref name="kokugakuin"/> The folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita]] likewise took ''tamayori-hime'' to mean "a consecrated woman to whom a spirit descends", and held that the close relationship between the two gave rise to belief in mother-and-son pairs of deities.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hosoi |first=Y. T. |date=1976 |title=The Sacred Tree in Japanese Prehistory |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1062238 |journal=History of Religions |volume=16 |issue=2 |pages=95–119 |issn=0018-2710}}</ref>

The Tamayori-hime of this article is written 玉依毘売 or 玉依毘売命 in the ''Kojiki'' and 玉依姫 in the ''Nihon Shoki''. She is the daughter of the sea god and the younger sister of Toyotama-bime, who bore Ugayafukiaezu to the heavenly grandson Hikohohodemi (Hoori). She married the nephew she had raised, Ugayafukiaezu, and bore Wakamikenu (Emperor Jimmu).<ref name="kotobank"/> Toshio Akima of the International Research Center for Japanese Studies considers it more likely that the two sisters are not separate figures but aspects of a single deity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Akima |first1=Toshio |date=1993 |title=The Origins of the Grand Shrine of Ise and the Cult of the Sun Goddess Amaterasu Ōmikami |journal=Japan Review |volume=4 |issue=4 |page=143 |issn=0915-0986 |jstor=25790929}}</ref>

The imperial line continues through grain spirits, and Tamayori-hime's sons are likewise Itsuse ("sacred rice"), Inahi ("rice spirit"), Mikenu ("lord of the offered food") and Wakamikenu ("young lord of the offered food"). The Tamayori-hime of this article is therefore thought to have been a shamaness possessed in particular by a grain spirit.<ref>{{cite book |author=[[Kazutami Nishimiya]] |title=Shinchō Nihon Koten Shūsei, vol. 27: Kojiki |date=1979-06-12 |publisher=[[Shinchosha]] |isbn=4106203278}}</ref>

Medieval shrine records say that Hime-gami, the goddess enshrined with Hachiman at [[Hachiman shrine]]s, is Tamayori-hime, daughter of the sea god and mother of Emperor Jimmu. Many identify Hime-gami with this Tamayori-hime on that basis, but there are other theories, including that she is a different Tamayori-hime.<ref name="kokugakuin"/>

== Genealogy ==
According to the ''Kiki'', her father is [[Watatsumi]]. Nothing is said of her mother. Her elder sister is [[Toyotama-hime]].

* Husband: '''[[Ugayafukiaezu]]''' (Hikonagisatake-ugayafukiaezu no Mikoto; in the ''Kojiki'' written 日子波限建鵜葺草葺不合命), ''Nihon Shoki''.
*: Son of Hoori.
** Son: [[Itsuse no Mikoto]] (Hiko-itsuse; Itsuse in the ''Kojiki''), ''Nihon Shoki''.
**: Died of an enemy's arrow during [[Jimmu's Eastern Expedition]].
** Son: [[Inahi no Mikoto]] (Inai; Inahi in the ''Kojiki''), ''Nihon Shoki''.
**: Crossed to the Korean peninsula; it is also said he became a ''sabimochi'' god (a shark god) during the Eastern Expedition.
** Son: [[Mikeiri no Mikoto]] (Mikenu; Mikenu in the ''Kojiki''), ''Nihon Shoki'', ''Sendai Kuji Hongi''.
**: Went to [[Tokoyo|Tokoyo no Kuni]] during the Eastern Expedition.
** Son: '''Kamu-yamato-iwarebiko''' (in the ''Kojiki'', Kamu-yamato-iwarebiko, personal name Wakamikenu), ''Nihon Shoki''.
**: Later '''[[Emperor Jimmu]]''', the first emperor.

== Records ==
=== Kojiki ===
According to the ''Kojiki'', after giving birth Toyotama-hime was ashamed at having shown her true form as a great shark, and left, abandoning her child Ugayafukiaezu. Later she sent her younger sister Tamayori-bime with a poem, and had her raise the child. Ugayafukiaezu later married Tamayori-bime, and she bore four sons.

=== Nihon Shoki ===
According to the ''Nihon Shoki'', Toyotama-hime came from the sea to the shore to bear Ugayafukiaezu, her child by Hoori, and was accompanied by her younger sister Tamayori-hime. Tamayori-hime later became the consort of Ugayafukiaezu, who from her point of view was her [[nephew]], and bore four sons.

The first variant account of the tenth section says that after the birth Toyotama-hime returned to the sea, leaving the child behind, and left Tamayori-hime to raise him.

The third variant account says that after the birth Toyotama-hime left the child and went into the sea, and later sent Tamayori-hime with a poem for Hoori and had her raise Ugayafukiaezu.

The fourth variant account gives, as "one version", that after the birth Toyotama-hime took the child in her own arms and went into the sea, but later had Tamayori-hime carry him and send him to the land.

=== Sendai Kuji Hongi ===
According to the ''[[Sendai Kuji Hongi]]'', after Toyotama-hime bore Ugayafukiaezu, Hoori's son, she took the child in her arms and went into the sea (or left Tamayori-hime to raise him and went away, and later had Tamayori-hime bring the child to the land). Later Toyotama-hime sent Tamayori-hime with a poem for Hoori and had her raise Ugayafukiaezu. At this time Takekuraki was born to Tamayori-hime and Hoori. Tamayori-hime later became the consort of Ugayafukiaezu, whom she had raised, and bore four sons.

== Hime-gami of the Hachiman shrines ==
Medieval shrine records, the ''Nijūissha-ki'', the ''Hachiman Usa-gū Gotakusenshū'', the ''Iwashimizu Hachimangū Massha-ki'' and the ''[[Hachiman Gudōkun]]'', say that Hime-gami, a goddess enshrined at Hachiman shrines (a consort goddess), is Tamayori-hime, daughter of the sea god and mother of Emperor Jimmu. Many identify Hime-gami with Jimmu's mother on this basis, but there are other theories: that she is the three [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata goddesses]], that she is an aunt of [[Emperor Ōjin]], that she is a fusion of these, or that she is a different, homonymous goddess, a fire goddess, and not Jimmu's mother.<ref name="kokugakuin"/>
